chunks: Shoot-through and dead time. The question: What happens if both the NFET and PFET are on at the same time? How do you avoid this?
Shoot-through happens when the top and bottom transistors are on at the same time.
That makes a direct short from the input to ground, so a huge current flows for a moment and wastes energy.
Dead time is the short pause between one transistor turning off and the other turning on, which prevents it.
Picture an airlock with two doors. The outer and inner doors must never be open together, or air rushes straight through.
The rule is: close one door completely, wait a moment, and only then open the other. For a short time both are shut. That brief gap is the dead time.
Both gates driven high. The only impedance between the supply and ground is R DS(on) 1 plus R DS(on) 2 plus connection and capacitor impedance.
The input capacitor, not the distant source, supplies the surge, so the loop through C in carries a multi-amp-to-tens-of-amps spike at the switching frequency.
Shoot-through: both transistors conducting at once, shorting the supply. Dead time: a deliberate gap with both transistors off.
Body diode: the built-in diode that carries the current during dead time ("Body diode in the off state, SW waveform").
Adaptive dead time: a controller that senses the gap and makes it as short as is safe. Switch node: the midpoint between the two transistors.
Use a 500 kilohertz buck, so the period is 2 microseconds, or 2000 nanoseconds. Add a 20 nanoseconds gap at each of the two transitions.
That is 40 nanoseconds of dead time per cycle, or 2 percent of the cycle.
The current in the gap flows through a body diode, which costs a little energy but is much cheaper than a short circuit. That is the whole idea.
"If both are on, V in is shorted to ground through two small R DS(on) s.
Real current is tens to hundreds of amps for nanoseconds, limited by saturation and the input cap, but it wastes energy every cycle, heats the FETs, droops V in and can destroy them.
Avoid it with dead time, ideally adaptive, or non-overlapping gate logic.
Also guard against dv/dt-induced turn-on through the Miller capacitance with a low-impedance turn-off, a gate resistor on turn-on, and safe power-up states."
